writtenQuestions.text:
A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below:

For each arrangement, complete the table by determining:
(i) the total extension in terms of x.
(ii) the spring constant in terms of k.

| Arrangement | Total Extension x | Spring constant (k) of the arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom.] | | |
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.] | | |
modelAnswer: For one spring, L = kx.
Series: each spring carries load L, so each extends by x.
Total extension in series = x + x = 2x.
Spring constant in series = L/(2x) = kx/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the identical springs share the load equally, so each carries L/2.
Extension of each spring = (L/2)/k = x/2; hence total extension = x/2.
Spring constant in parallel = L/(x/2) = 2L/x = 2k.

rubric.why: In parallel, the load is shared equally, so each spring extends by x/2 and the bar moves that distance.

rubric.why: Two parallel springs have the combined effect of both spring constants.

explain.title: Deforming force
explain.body: Your textbook defines a deforming force as an external force applied on an object that can change its size or shape. Stretching a spring increases its length; compression reduces it.

explain.title: Elasticity
explain.body: Your textbook defines an elastic object as: “An object is said to be elastic, if after removal of the deforming force, it restores to its original size and shape.” The property of the material is called elasticity.

explain.title: Inelastic materials and elastic limit
explain.body: Some materials, such as clay dough or plasticine, do not return to their original shape after the deforming force is removed; your textbook calls them inelastic materials. Beyond the elastic limit, the change becomes permanent and the material does not regain its original shape or size.

explain.title: Spring constant
explain.body: For a spring, spring constant is force divided by extension: k = F/x. Use force in newtons and extension in metres to obtain k in N m⁻¹. A larger k means more force is needed for the same extension.

Reversing the spring-constant formula: use k = F/x, not x/F.
Giving a Hooke's law statement without specifying the range in which force and extension are proportional.

explain.title: Hooke’s law
explain.body: If a force F is applied on a spring to stretch or compress it, the extension or compression x has been found directly proportional to the applied force within the elastic limit. Thus, F ∝ x or F = kx or k = F/x.

explain.title: Spring constant and stiffness
explain.body: where k is the constant of proportionality and is known as spring constant. In fact, it is a measure of stiffness of the spring. The greater the value of spring constant, the greater will be the stiffness or strength of the spring. Its unit is N m⁻¹.

explain.title: Force-extension graph
explain.body: A graph of force against extension is a straight line passing through the origin. The gradient or slope of force-extension graph is a measure of spring constant k. If the load exceeds the elastic limit, the spring is permanently deformed and the graph will no longer remain linear.

explain.title: Applications
explain.body: Springs are used in spring scales, the balance wheel of mechanical clocks and galvanometers. A spring scale measures weight from extension or compression; a clock spring controls back-and-forth motion; and a galvanometer’s hair spring helps restore its pointer to zero.

explain.title: What density means
explain.body: Density of a substance is defined as its mass per unit volume. This means density compares the mass of a substance with the space it occupies.

explain.title: The formula and units
explain.body: Density = Mass/Volume. The SI unit of density is kg m⁻³. Another unit in use is g cm⁻³. Keep the mass and volume units consistent when calculating.

explain.title: Finding the volume of a solid
explain.body: For a regular solid, measure its dimensions and calculate its volume. For an irregular solid, place it in a liquid in a measuring cylinder; the rise in the liquid level gives the volume of the solid.

explain.title: Why substances have different densities
explain.body: Equal volumes of different substances can have different masses. Their molecules differ in size and mass, and their intermolecular spacing differs. A substance with more closely packed and heavier molecules has more mass in the same volume.

explain.title: Meaning of pressure
explain.body: Pressure is defined as the force exerted normally on unit area of an object.

explain.title: Formula and unit
explain.body: If F is the force acting normally on a surface of area A, then pressure P on the surface is given by P = F/A. The SI unit is N m⁻² and is called pascal (Pa).

explain.title: Contact area changes pressure
explain.body: The area A on which the force acts is usually referred as contact area. For a certain force, the pressure can be very large if the contact area A is small.

explain.title: Everyday examples
explain.body: A sharp chopper edge and the sharp end of a thumb pin have small contact areas, so they produce high pressure. Pebbles also reduce the foot's contact area and make walking painful. Broad, flat elephant feet increase contact area and reduce pressure.

explain.title: Pressure comes from the liquid above
explain.body: Imagine a patch of area A at depth h. The liquid column above it has volume V = Ah and mass m = ρAh. Its weight acts on that patch.

explain.title: The liquid-pressure equation
explain.body: The force from the liquid column is F = mg = ρAhg. Dividing by area gives P = F/A = ρgh. The area cancels, so pressure depends on depth and density, not the patch's area.

explain.title: Greater depth means greater pressure
explain.body: Since P = ρgh, for the same liquid and gravity, increasing h increases pressure. That is why water from a lower hole spurts out with greater pressure.

explain.title: Pressure acts normally
explain.body: Pressure produces force at right angle to a surface. A force or its component that is parallel to the surface does not contribute to pressure.

explain.title: Pressure in a liquid spreads
explain.body: When a water-filled bag is squeezed, water squirts from its holes in different directions. This demonstrates that pressure is transmitted throughout the liquid.

explain.title: What atmospheric pressure means
explain.body: The Earth is surrounded by air called the atmosphere. Air molecules move and collide with objects. Your textbook defines it this way: “This force per unit area is the atmospheric pressure.”

explain.title: Pressure acts in all directions
explain.body: Air molecules move randomly and collide with objects from different directions. Your textbook states: “Since the molecules of air have random motion, therefore, atmospheric pressure acts equally in all directions.”

explain.title: Pressure at sea level
explain.body: At sea level, atmospheric pressure is about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. Your textbook calls this value standard atmospheric pressure.

explain.title: Atmospheric pressure changes with height
explain.body: Air density decreases with altitude, and atmospheric pressure decreases as we go higher. Your textbook gives about 55 kPa at 5 km and 1 kPa at 30 km. Lower atmospheric pressure means greater altitude.

explain.title: Evidence of atmospheric pressure
explain.body: In the tin-can activity, steam condenses as the can cools. The pressure inside falls, and the outside atmospheric pressure pushes the can inward.

mistakes: Do not say atmospheric pressure acts only downward; it acts equally in all directions.
Do not confuse pressure with force: pressure is force per unit area.
Do not say atmospheric pressure increases with altitude; it decreases as altitude increases.

explain.title: What a barometer measures
explain.body: “Atmospheric pressure is usually measured by the height of mercury column which it can support.” Instruments which measure the atmospheric pressure are called barometers.

explain.title: How the simple mercury barometer works
explain.body: A tube closed at one end is filled with mercury and inverted in a dish of mercury. The space above the mercury is completely empty, so its pressure is almost zero. A scale beside the tube measures the column height.

explain.title: Why the column represents atmospheric pressure
explain.body: Points A and B are at the same level in the mercury, so their pressures are equal. The pressure at the mercury surface in the dish is atmospheric pressure, and the liquid-column pressure is P = ρgh.

explain.title: Pressure and weather
explain.body: Atmospheric pressure changes with conditions. At high altitudes air is less dense and pressure falls. More water vapour also lowers air density, so low pressure in cloudy regions can warn that rain may follow.

writtenQuestions.text: Example 6.4: The diameters of the pistons of a hydraulic press are 5 cm and 25 cm respectively. A normal force of 160 N is applied on the smaller piston, what will be the pressure exerted by this force on the bigger piston? How much weight can be lifted by the other piston?
modelAnswer: Let the areas of cross-sections of the pistons be A₁ and A₂ and their radii be r₁ and r₂ respectively.
A₁ = πr₁² and A₂ = πr₂²
F₁ = 160 N
According to Pascal's law, F₁/A₁ = w/A₂
w = F₁A₂/A₁ = F₁πr₂²/(πr₁²) = F₁ × r₂²/r₁²
Pressure transmitted = 8.15 × 10⁴ Pa; weight lifted = 4000 N = 4 kN.

explain.title: Pascal's law
explain.body: The textbook states: “When pressure is applied at one point in an enclosed fluid, it is transmitted equally to all parts of fluid without loss.” A fluid includes a liquid or a gas. This means pressure applied at one point is passed on throughout the enclosed fluid.

explain.title: Hydraulic press
explain.body: In a hydraulic press, a small piston pushes on an incompressible liquid. The liquid transmits the pressure to a larger piston. Since the larger piston has a greater area, the force on it is greater: F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁.

explain.title: Hydraulic brakes
explain.body: Pushing the brake pedal applies pressure to liquid in the master cylinder. Pascal's law transmits this pressure through the brake fluid to larger pistons at the wheels. Those pistons press brake pads towards the discs or drums, and friction slows the vehicle.

mistakes: Do not say pressure is transmitted only downwards; Pascal's law says it is transmitted equally to all parts of the enclosed fluid.
Do not reverse the piston-area ratio. From F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, the output force is F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁.
Do not confuse force with pressure: pressure is force divided by area.
Convert areas to m² when the answer for pressure is required in N m⁻².
Include the unit in the final answer and show the equation and substitution.

explain.title: Pressure
explain.body: Pressure is force per unit area: p = F/A. For the same force, a smaller area produces greater pressure. Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².

explain.title: Pressure in liquids and the atmosphere
explain.body: Liquid pressure is given by p = ρgh, so it depends on density, depth and gravity. Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of the air above us. A mercury barometer measures it by balancing atmospheric pressure against a mercury column.

explain.title: Pascal's law
explain.body: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted unchanged to every part of the fluid and the walls of its container. Hydraulic presses, lifts and brakes use this law.

explain.title: Elasticity and Hooke's law
explain.body: Elasticity is the ability of a solid to regain its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed. Hooke's law states that extension is directly proportional to applied force, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded: F = kx.

explain.title: Springs and pressure calculations
explain.body: Springs in series extend more under the same load; parallel springs share the load and have a greater combined spring constant. In calculations, convert measurements to SI units before substituting into a formula.

Applying Hooke's law beyond the elastic limit.
In hydraulic calculations, mixing up the small and large piston areas or pairing an area with the wrong force.
Leaving out units or giving an answer with the wrong unit.

notes.title: How forces deform solids
notes.answer: Elasticity is the property by which a material restores its original size and shape after the deforming force is removed.
notes.explanation: A deforming force can change an object's size or shape. Elastic materials return to their original size and shape when the force is removed. For a spring, the spring constant tells us how much force is needed for each unit of extension.
notes.simple: Push, pull or squeeze something and its shape or size may change. If it returns to its original shape when you stop, it is elastic.
examples: A spring stretches when a load is hung from it and returns to its original length when the load is removed.
A tennis ball and the racket strings deform when the ball is hit; they regain their original shapes after the ball bounces away.
steps: A force that changes an object's size or shape is called a deforming force.
A spring can be stretched (extended) or squeezed (compressed).
An object is elastic if it restores its original size and shape after the deforming force is removed.
The property that allows it to do this is called elasticity.
For a spring, spring constant is calculated using k = F/x, where F is force and x is extension.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to an elastic object when its deforming force is removed?
notes.checkAnswer: An elastic object returns to its original size and shape after the deforming force is removed.

notes.title: Hooke’s law and spring constant
notes.answer: F = kx; the spring constant is k = F/x and is measured in N m⁻¹.
notes.explanation: Within the elastic limit, a spring’s extension or compression is directly proportional to the force applied to it. The spring constant tells us how stiff the spring is.
notes.simple: A stiffer spring needs more force for the same stretch.
examples: If a 10 N force stretches a spring by 0.02 m, k = F/x = 10/0.02 = 500 N m⁻¹.
For a spring with k = 200 N m⁻¹ stretched by 0.03 m, F = kx = 200 × 0.03 = 6 N.
steps: Write the relation: F = kx.
Substitute the force and extension, using extension in metres.
To find k, use k = F/x; to find F, use F = kx.
Give the unit of k as N m⁻¹.

notes.title: Finding density
notes.explanation: Density tells us how much mass is packed into a certain volume. Find it by dividing mass by volume.
notes.simple: Density is a way of comparing how much matter is packed into the same amount of space.
examples: A mass of 90 g in a volume of 10 cm³ has density 90 g ÷ 10 cm³ = 9 g cm⁻³.
If a solid raises water from 40 cm³ to 44 cm³, its volume is 4 cm³.
steps: Find the mass of the substance.
Find its volume.
Divide mass by volume: Density = Mass/Volume.
Write the answer with an appropriate density unit.

notes.title: Pressure
notes.answer: Pressure is the force exerted normally on unit area of an object. Its formula is P = F/A.
notes.explanation: Pressure tells us how much normal force acts on each unit of contact area. The same force produces more pressure on a smaller area.
notes.simple: Pressure is force spread over an area. A smaller area means greater pressure for the same force.
examples: A sharp chopper blade cuts easily because its small contact area produces high pressure.
An elephant's broad feet spread its weight over a large area, reducing pressure on the ground.
steps: Write the formula: P = F/A.
Use the force acting normally on the surface for F.
Use the contact area for A.
Calculate pressure and write the unit in pascals (Pa).
notes.checkQuestion: If the same force acts on a smaller area, what happens to the pressure?
notes.checkAnswer: Pressure increases when the same force acts on a smaller area.

notes.title: Pressure in liquids
notes.explanation: Liquid pressure is caused by the weight of the liquid above a point. It depends on the liquid's density and the depth of the point. Pressure pushes at right angles to a surface.
notes.simple: The deeper you go in a liquid, the more liquid is above you, so the pressure is greater.
examples: At the same depth, a denser liquid produces more pressure.
The lowest hole in a water-filled container has the greatest pressure.
steps: Find the depth h below the liquid surface.
Use the liquid density ρ and gravitational acceleration g.
Substitute in P = ρgh, using SI units.
Give pressure in pascals (Pa), or N m⁻².

notes.title: Atmospheric Pressure
notes.answer: Atmospheric pressure is the force per unit area exerted by the atmosphere.
notes.explanation: Air molecules move randomly and collide with objects. These collisions exert force over an area, creating atmospheric pressure. This pressure acts in all directions and decreases as altitude increases.
notes.simple: Air presses on us from every direction. The higher you go, the less air is above you, so the pressure is lower.
examples: At sea level, atmospheric pressure is about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.
When steam in a closed tin can cools and condenses, the outside atmospheric pressure can crush the can.
steps: Remember: pressure is force per unit area.
Air molecules collide with objects and exert force.
The force per unit area caused by the atmosphere is atmospheric pressure.
Atmospheric pressure is greatest at sea level and decreases with altitude.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to atmospheric pressure as altitude increases?
notes.checkAnswer: Atmospheric pressure decreases as altitude increases.

notes.title: Measuring Atmospheric Pressure
notes.answer: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure using the height of a mercury column.
notes.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of a mercury column. Air pressure supports the mercury, and changes in atmospheric pressure can help forecast weather.
notes.simple: Air presses on the mercury in the dish and holds up a column of mercury in the barometer tube. A higher column means greater atmospheric pressure.
examples: At sea level, the textbook gives a mercury column height of 760 mm.
If water replaced mercury in a barometer, the column would need to be about 10.3 m high.
steps: Fill a glass tube, closed at one end, completely with mercury.
Invert the tube vertically in a dish of mercury.
Measure the height of the mercury column with a scale.
Use the column height to find the atmospheric pressure.
notes.checkAnswer: Atmospheric pressure supports the mercury column; pressure at the same level in the mercury is equal.

notes.title: Reading a simple manometer
notes.answer: A simple manometer compares the pressure of a gas with atmospheric pressure by showing the difference between the mercury levels.
notes.explanation: A manometer compares the pressure of a gas with atmospheric pressure. The difference between the mercury levels shows whether the gas pressure is greater or less than atmospheric pressure.
notes.simple: Think of the two mercury levels as a pressure comparison: the gas pushes mercury down in its arm when its pressure is greater.
examples: If mercury is lower in the arm connected to the gas, the gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
If mercury is higher in the arm connected to the gas, the gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
steps: Check which arm is connected to the gas and which arm is open.
Compare the mercury levels in the two arms.
If mercury is lower in the gas-connected arm, gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
If mercury is higher in the gas-connected arm, gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
notes.checkQuestion: A gas is connected to one arm of a manometer. Mercury is lower in that arm than in the open arm. Is the gas pressure greater or less than atmospheric pressure?
notes.checkAnswer: The gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.

notes.title: Pascal's Law
notes.answer: When pressure is applied at one point in an enclosed fluid, it is transmitted equally to all parts of fluid without loss.
notes.explanation: Pascal's law explains how pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is passed on throughout the fluid. Hydraulic machines use this to transfer force and, with a larger output piston, produce a greater force.
notes.simple: Push on a fluid in a closed system, and the pressure is passed on equally through the fluid.
examples: A hydraulic press uses pressure from a small piston to produce a larger force on a large piston.
In hydraulic brakes, pressure from the brake pedal is transmitted through brake fluid to pistons at the wheels.
steps: Use Pascal's law: pressure is transmitted equally to all parts of an enclosed fluid.
For a piston, pressure is force divided by area: P = F/A.
Set the pressures at the two pistons equal: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
Rearrange to find the unknown force or area.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to pressure applied at one point in an enclosed fluid?
notes.checkAnswer: The pressure is transmitted equally to every part of the enclosed fluid.

notes.title: Pressure, liquids and elasticity
notes.explanation: Pressure is force acting on each unit of area. In a liquid, pressure increases with depth and depends on the liquid's density and gravity. Pascal's law explains how pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted throughout it. Springs obey Hooke's law while they remain within their elastic limit.
notes.simple: Pressure tells us how concentrated a force is. A small area gives greater pressure for the same force. Liquids also press more strongly at greater depths.
examples: A sharp knife has a small contact area, so the same force produces greater pressure.
A hydraulic press uses pressure transmitted through an enclosed liquid to multiply force.
steps: For pressure, use pressure = force ÷ area.
For liquid pressure, use p = ρgh.
For a spring within its elastic limit, use F = kx.
For connected hydraulic pistons, equate their pressures: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
Write the final answer with its correct unit.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to liquid pressure as depth increases?
notes.checkAnswer: Liquid pressure increases with depth; it also depends on the liquid's density and gravity.

written.text:
A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below:

For each arrangement, complete the table by determining:
(i) the total extension in terms of x.
(ii) the spring constant in terms of k.

| Arrangement | Total Extension x | Spring constant (k) of the arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom.] | | |
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.] | | |
modelAnswer: For one spring, L = kx.
Series: each spring carries load L, so each extends by x.
Total extension in series = x + x = 2x.
Spring constant in series = L/(2x) = kx/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the identical springs share the load equally, so each carries L/2.
Extension of each spring = (L/2)/k = x/2; hence total extension = x/2.
Spring constant in parallel = L/(x/2) = 2L/x = 2k.

written.text: Example 6.4: The diameters of the pistons of a hydraulic press are 5 cm and 25 cm respectively. A normal force of 160 N is applied on the smaller piston, what will be the pressure exerted by this force on the bigger piston? How much weight can be lifted by the other piston?

Q6.1. A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below:

For each arrangement, complete the table by determining:
(i) the total extension in terms of x.
(ii) the spring constant in terms of k.

| Arrangement | Total Extension x | Spring constant (k) of the arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom.] | | |
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.] | | |
modelAnswer: One spring under load L extends by x, so L = kx.
Series: the same load acts on each spring, so each extends by x.
Series total extension = x + x = 2x; equivalent k = L/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the load is shared equally, so each spring supports L/2.
Extension of each spring = (L/2)/k = x/2; both have the same total extension x/2.
Parallel equivalent spring constant = L/(x/2) = 2k.

written.text: Q6.9. Comment on the statement. “Density is a property of a material not the property of an object made of that material.”
modelAnswer: The statement is correct.
For a particular material under the same conditions, density is characteristic of the material; it does not depend on the size or shape of an object made from it.

written.text: Q6.1. What is Hooke’s law? Give three applications of this law.
modelAnswer: Hooke's law states that extension is directly proportional to applied force, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.
Mathematically, F ∝ x, or F = kx.
Applications include a spring balance, suspension springs in vehicles and spring-based weighing machines.

written.text: Q6.5. Explain that atmosphere exerts pressure. What are its applications? Give at least three examples.
modelAnswer: The atmosphere has weight, and its weight exerts pressure on the Earth's surface and on objects.
When pressure inside a straw is reduced by sucking, atmospheric pressure pushes the drink up the straw.
A syringe draws liquid in when pressure inside it is reduced.
A suction cup sticks to a surface because atmospheric pressure presses it against the surface.

written.text: Q6.9. The area of cross-section of the small and large pistons of a hydraulic press is respectively 10 cm² and 100 cm². What force should be exerted on the small piston in order to lift a car of weight 4000 N?
modelAnswer: Given: A₁ = 10 cm², A₂ = 100 cm², F₂ = 4000 N.
By Pascal's law, F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
F₁ = F₂A₁/A₂ = (4000 N × 10 cm²)/(100 cm²).
Force on the small piston, F₁ = 400 N.
